title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbooks, Benchmarks, Runbooks
author: Asha Ramanathan
content:
Summary:
This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling heuristics, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks for the Redwood Inference serving runtime. It is intended for engineers on the Serving Runtime, SRE, and Performance teams and for anyone performing performance triage, model onboarding, or capacity planning.

1) High-level runtime architecture
Overview:
- Service name: rdinference-runtime (microservice group: runtime-core).
- Primary responsibilities: model loading, tokenizer/vocab management, KV-cache lifecycle, attention/sequence execution, batching, prefix caching, and quantized execution paths.
- Deploy modes: hosted (multi-tenant), dedicated (tenant pools), private (VPC).

Components and flow:
1. Ingress (api-gateway) — authenticates, rate-limits, enforces per-route SLOs.
2. Router (smart-router) — routes requests by policy: latency-priority, cost-priority, regional affinity, tenant-isolation.
3. Dispatcher (request-dispatch) — assigns request to worker group based on model family, sequence length, and cached prefixes.
4. Worker (runtime-worker) — GPU process responsible for kernel execution, KV cache, and streaming response generation.
5. Cache Layer (prefix-kv-cache) — Redis-like LRU with per-tenant partitioning; persistent across short-lived workers.
6. Telemetry (runtime-metrics) — exports per-token latency, GPU utilization, memory high-water marks, OOM counters.

SLOs and targets (global):
- P99 token generation latency (interactive profile): <= 150ms (per-token)
- P50 end-to-end response latency (seq <= 512 tokens): <= 200ms
- Availability (runtime-core): 99.95% per month
- OOM rate: < 0.05% of requests

Owners:
- Runtime architecture: eng/serving-runtime (primary owner: Asha Ramanathan)
- Kernel scheduling: eng/serving-runtime/kernels (owner: Liam Chen)
- Profiling & benchmarks: eng/perf (owner: Marisol Vega)

2) Kernel scheduling heuristics
Goals:
- Maximize throughput while respecting latency SLOs and per-tenant isolation.
- Avoid GPU memory fragmentation and reduce OOMs.

Key heuristics and rules:
- Topology-aware placement: prefer colocating same-model shards on GPUs with similar memory headroom.
- Dynamic batch windows: worker increases batching-window only if 95th percentile request queue wait < 20ms and observed latency headroom exists.
- KV-cache affinity: requests that hit an L1 prefix cache are scheduled onto workers with that cache hot to avoid remote cache fetches.
- Quantized-path routing: for requests flagged cost-priority, the router may select a quantized model variant (e.g., q4_k_m) if quality gating passes.

Scheduling knobs (config examples):
- max_batch_tokens: 4096
- max_batch_size: 64
- batching_latency_target_ms: 12
- kv_cache_affinity_window_ms: 200
- gc_interval_ms: 120000

(See Appendix: runtime-config.yaml snippet)

3) Profiling playbook (how to profile a regression)
Prerequisites:
- Access to perf cluster (role: eng-perf), metrics in Grafana, traces in Tempo, perf traces in perf-trace-store.
- A representative workload or the failing prompt set.

Step-by-step profiling procedure:
1. Reproduce: Use curl or the inference-scaffold to reproduce the regression against a canary model + commit. Example:
   curl -X POST https://canary-api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -d '{"model":"gpt-mini-2026-canary","input":"{PROMPT}"}'
2. Snapshot traces: Enable detailed tracing for request-id (DEBUG) for 10–30 requests. Command (ops CLI):
   opscli trace start --service runtime-worker --request-id <RERequestID> --duration 30s
3. Collect GPU profiles: On worker node run: nvprof or nsight CLI capture (non-prod only):
   sudo nsight-sys --capture-range=timer --output /tmp/trace.sqz -- target_pid=<pid>
4. Collect CPU flamegraphs: run perf and generate collapsed stack:
   sudo perf record -F 99 -g --pid=<pid> -- sleep 10
   sudo perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
   ./flamegraph.pl out.folded > cpu.svg
5. Analyze: correlate service traces (Tempo) with GPU kernel timelines and flamegraphs to identify long kernels, memory copies, or serialization points.
6. Mitigate: if hot path is kernel A on attention, open an ADR to modify kernel selection or reorder data movement. If GC pressure, tune gc_interval_ms or increase worker memory.
7. Validate: re-run 95th/99th latency benchmarks (see benchmarking suite) and confirm regression resolved.

Profiling checklist (quick):
- Repro steps documented
- Request-level traces captured
- GPU profiles captured
- CPU flamegraphs captured
- Config snapshot attached
- Runbook/owner and JIRA ticket linked

4) Benchmarking suite (how we measure perf and cost)
Bench types:
- Microbench: single-kernel latency and memory tests (used during kernel dev).
- Throughput bench: steady-state token/sec at target latency SLOs.
- End-to-end bench: includes network, tokenization, and response streaming.
- Regression bench: periodic canonical prompt-set to detect quality/perf drift.

Key artifacts:
- bench-suite repo: git@internal:redwood/bench-suite.git (branch: main).
- canonical-prompt-sets: workloads/interactive-512.json, workloads/batch-2048.json.
- CI integration: bench-suite runs nightly against stable and candidate images; failures create a perf-alert PR.

Acceptance criteria for a change (example):
- No P95 latency regression > 5% for interactive workloads.
- Throughput per-GPU change within +/-7% baseline for high-throughput models.

Running a benchmark (example command):
- benchcli run --suite end-to-end --model gpt-large-2026 --concurrency 16 --seq-len 512 --duration 300s

Metrics collected:
- token/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency (per-token and end-to-end), GPU utilization, GPU SM efficiency, memory high-water, OOMs, CPU steal. Results are stored in bench-results bucket with tags for model, image, git-sha.

5) Release notes (recent items)
- 2026-02-15 (v2026.2.15): Kernel selector improvement — reduced P99 token latency by 8% for attention-heavy workloads; enabled topology-aware placement by default (rollout: canary -> 100% over 2 days).
- 2026-01-28 (v2026.1.28): KV-cache affinity optimization — reduced remote-cache fetches by 42% in dedicated pools.
- 2025-12-12 (v2025.12.12): Added quantized routing flag and quality gate for q4_k_m models.

Rollout guidance:
1. Canary (1–3 pods) for 2 hours with synthetic traffic at multiple seq-len points.
2. Gradual ramp: 10% -> 50% -> 100% over 48–72 hours while monitoring P95/P99 and OOMs.
3. Automatic rollback if P99 increases > 10% or OOMs spike > 0.1% above baseline.

6) Known issues (operational)
- ISSUE-001 (status: open): Occasional GPU memory fragmentation causing OOMs after prolonged small-batch workloads (repro rate: ~0.02%). Workaround: periodic worker restart every 6 hours; mitigation: gc_interval tuning and upcoming allocator patch. Owner: eng/serving-runtime.
- ISSUE-002 (status: investigating): Inconsistent batch-window growth under bursty traffic — leads to higher P99 under certain tail traffic patterns. Temporary workaround: set batching_latency_target_ms=8 on impacted pools.
- ISSUE-003 (status: fixed in v2026.2.15): Rare kernel selector mis-route for multihead-attention variant on GPU A100-80GB.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)
A. Incident: High P99 token latency
1. Triage: run runtimectl diagnostics --since 5m --service runtime-worker; check p99_token_latency, gpu_util, queue_depth.
2. If p99_token_latency > SLA threshold (configured per-customer):
   a. Identify affected models and pools with: runtimectl top --metric p99_token_latency --since 10m
   b. If a single model: scale up workers for affected pool: autoscalectl set --pool <pool> --replicas +2
   c. If many models: switch routing policy to latency-priority for the region: routerctl set-policy --region <r> latency-priority
3. Collect traces and escalate to oncall with logs attached (Slack channel #oncall-runtime and Pager duty: runtime-oncall).
4. Post-incident: fill postmortem template and link bench runs before/after.

B. Incident: Repeated OOMs on worker
1. Confirm OOMs: runtimectl metrics query --name oom_count --since 1h
2. If OOM count spikes: drain worker: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --grace-period=60
3. Increase worker memory class or reduce max_batch_size for pool.
4. Re-provision node with updated kernel/allocator if fix available.

C. Runbook: Performance regression detected by CI
1. CI creates perf-alert PR with bench result diff.
2. Perf owner triages using bench-results and tracing artifacts.
3. If change is code-related, create changelist referencing kernels and include microbench results.

-----BEGIN YAML-----
service: rdinference-runtime
max_batch_tokens: "4096"
max_batch_size: "64"
batching_latency_target_ms: "12"
kv_cache_affinity_window_ms: "200"
quantized_routing_enabled: "true"
gc_interval_ms: "120000"
-----END YAML-----

Appendix B: Quick CLI snippets
- Start a local worker with debug log level:
   ./runtime-worker --model-path /models/gpt-mini --log-level debug --max-batch-size 8
- Run microbench for kernel attention optimization:
   benchcli micro --kernel attention --model gpt-mini --iterations 1000
